stem: A 62-year-old man presents with rectal bleeding and unintentional weight loss. On a digital rectal exam, a mass is palpated 10 cm from the anal verge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Rectal bleeding + weight loss + a palpable mass 10 cm from the anal verge in a 62-year-old = rectal cancer.

why.A: Haemorrhoids don't form a mass at 10 cm or cause weight loss.
why.C: A fissure is at the anal verge and painful.
why.D: Diverticulosis has no palpable rectal mass.

stem: A 52-year-old patient presents with right lower quadrant pain and weight loss. CT scan shows a mass involving the appendix and cecum. Colonoscopy reveals a suspicious lesion, and biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma. What is the most appropriate management?
expl: Adenocarcinoma involving the appendix and caecum → right hemicolectomy (oncological resection with the ileocolic pedicle and nodes).

why.A: Appendectomy doesn't clear the caecal tumour or nodes.
why.C: Correct.

stem: A patient with colorectal cancer is being evaluated for tumor recurrence. What is the most appropriate tumor marker to assess recurrence?
expl: CEA is the colorectal cancer marker used to detect recurrence after resection (a rise suggests recurrence).

why.C: CA 19-9 = pancreatobiliary.

stem: familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) should start sigmoidoscopy screening. What is the recommended age? ( not exactly but same idea)
srcNote: The check mark is reproduced from the source; no separate answer key is provided.
expl: FAP: annual sigmoidoscopy/colonoscopy starting at 10–12 years in at-risk children (polyps appear in the teens); prophylactic surgery usually late teens–early 20s.

why.C: Too late — polyps may already be numerous.

stem: patient presents for screening colonoscopy. The patient has no family history of colon cancer. What is the most appropriate recommendation for age to do colonoscopy ?

opts.t: Screening colonoscopy every 10 years at age 45- 50

expl: Average-risk adults start colorectal screening at 45 (older guidelines 50); colonoscopy is repeated every 10 years if normal. Age 40 is for those with a first-degree relative (or 10 years before the relative's diagnosis).

why.B: That start age is for increased-risk (family history) patients.

stem: A male with long-standing ulcerative colitis (>10 years) is diagnosed with adenocarcinoma in the sigmoid colon. What is the best surgical option?
srcNote: The check mark is reproduced from the source; no separate answer key is provided.
expl: Cancer in long-standing UC → the whole colon and rectum are at risk (field change, synchronous lesions) → (restorative) proctocolectomy.

why.C: Segmental resection leaves diseased mucosa.

stem: A patient is diagnosed with both sigmoid and rectal cancer. What type of resection is most appropriate?
srcNote: No answer key is stated in the source. Only three options are supplied in the source.
expl: The source had no key. Synchronous sigmoid and (upper/mid) rectal cancers can be removed in one specimen by an anterior resection (sigmoid + rectum with mesorectum). APR is only for low rectal tumours involving the sphincters.

why.C: APR removes the anus unnecessarily unless the tumour is very low.

stem: Anatomy — which parts of the bowel are supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery?
ansText: The hindgut — distal third of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon and upper rectum (via the left colic, sigmoid and superior rectal arteries).

stem: What is the definition of Lynch syndrome (Amsterdam criteria)?
ansText: Amsterdam "3-2-1" rule: at least 3 relatives with Lynch-associated cancer (colorectal, endometrial…), one a first-degree relative of the other two; at least 2 successive generations affected; at least 1 diagnosed before age 50; FAP excluded.

stem: A 20-year-old man, otherwise healthy, presented to the outpatient department complaining of per-rectal bleeding for 3 months. Anorectal examination showed 3rd degree hemorrhoids. He has a family history of Colon cancer and Symptoms of Iron deficiency anemia. Which of the following is the appropriate next step in management?
expl: Rectal bleeding with iron-deficiency anaemia and a family history of colon cancer → colonoscopy to exclude a proximal lesion before attributing bleeding to haemorrhoids.

why.A: Treating the haemorrhoids first could miss cancer.
why.B: Treating the haemorrhoids first could miss cancer.
why.C: Upper endoscopy isn't first for fresh rectal bleeding.

stem: 89 year old patient presents with 3 day history of inability to pass flatus, she previously had 5 months constipation imaging revealed obstruction in sigmoid colon with no distended small bowel. She has multiple liver and lung metastases. What is the management
expl: Source key: colectomy — a palliative resection of the obstructing sigmoid tumor relieves the obstruction and prevents bleeding/perforation; many would also accept a stent or colostomy in an 89-year-old with metastases. Follow the source key for the exam.

why.C: A defunctioning colostomy is a reasonable alternative.
why.D: A stent is another palliative option, especially in frail patients.

stem: rectal carcinoid (not cancer) :
expl: Neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumours secrete chromogranin A — the general NET marker (with 5-HIAA for serotonin-secreting tumours). CEA is for adenocarcinoma.

why.C: PSA = prostate.

stem: A 37 year old man with a 10 year history of ulcerative colitis who has been found to have a sessile polyp 10 cm from the anal verge with high-grade dysplasia Which one of the following is the most appropriate surgical procedure?
expl: High-grade dysplasia in long-standing UC → the whole colorectal mucosa is at risk → restorative total proctocolectomy with ileal J-pouch (removes all diseased mucosa, preserves continence).

why.B: Local excision leaves the field at risk.
why.C: Leaves the rectum (still diseased).

stem: 60 year old patient presented with PR bleeding and weight loss. DRE was done and a mass was palpated 10 way from the anal verge. Colonoscopy with biopsy confirmed adenocarcinoma. CT CAP showed NO distant met. Pelvic MRI showed invasion of the pericolic fat (T3N1 MO). Which of the following is the management of choice?
srcNote: (Colorectal cancer) Other source key (Final 436 F Q24): Answer: D not sure. In that version: D. Neo-adjuvant followed by surgery.
expl: Mid rectal cancer (10 cm) T3N1M0 → neoadjuvant (chemo)radiotherapy first to down-stage and reduce local recurrence, then total mesorectal excision (LAR), then chemotherapy. Another version keyed "neoadjuvant followed by surgery".

why.B: Chemotherapy alone doesn't control the pelvis.
why.C: Correct.
why.D: Sigmoid resection is the wrong operation.

stem: 54 yo male during colonoscopy sessile polyp is found. Histological features confirm malignant polyp Adenocarcinoma with ..... free margin, What you will do next?

opts.t: follow up ____ ( forgot duration ) with residual tissue
follow up since there is a margin

srcNote: (Colorectal Cancer) The source recall is incomplete, including the margin detail and follow-up duration. Gaps are retained as written.
expl: Keyed segmental resection — a malignant sessile polyp (Haggitt level 4 = submucosal invasion) carries a significant nodal risk, so formal oncological resection is usually needed unless all favourable features (clear margin ≥ 2 mm, well/moderately differentiated, no LVI, no budding) are present.

why.B: Repeat endoscopic resection doesn't address the nodes.
why.C: Follow-up alone is for favourable pedunculated malignant polyps.
why.D: A margin alone isn't enough for a sessile malignant polyp.

stem: A 50 pt presented after sigmoidectomy, his staging is T3N0 with only 6 lymph nodes seen. Which of the following is the management of choice?
expl: Stage II (T3N0) with only 6 nodes examined (< 12) = inadequate staging → high-risk stage II → adjuvant chemotherapy.

why.C: Radiotherapy isn't used for colon cancer.
why.D: Inadequate nodes make him high risk.

stem: A 65-year-old male presented to the emergency room with a picture of bowel obstruction. A CT scan of the abdomen showed an ultra low rectal mass with bi-lobar liver metastasis, lung metastasis as well as retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Which or the following is the best management option for his current condition?
expl: Obstruction from an ultra-low rectal mass with widespread metastases → palliate the obstruction with a diverting stoma. Ultra-low tumors are not suitable for stents (tenesmus, pain, migration).

why.C: Stents are poor for ultra-low rectal tumors.

stem: In the management of colorectal cancer, what is CEA most useful for?

opts.t: To assess the prognosis of colorectal cancer
To assess severity of cancer aggressiveness
For surveillance of recurrent colorectal cancer

expl: CEA is not sensitive/specific enough for screening; its main use is follow-up for recurrence.

why.B: A high pre-op CEA has prognostic value, but the main use is surveillance.
why.C: Not a measure of aggressiveness.

stem: A 60-year-old woman complains of feeling tired while doing her usual household work over the last 3 months. She has been short of breath climbing one flight of stairs at home with increasing abdominal distension. Her haemoglobin is 8.5 g/L. Abdominal examination reveals a mobile mass in the right iliac fossa. Abdominal X-ray was done (image) What is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: (colorectal cancer) The source mentions an X-ray image, but no image is supplied with this question.
expl: Fatigue, breathlessness from anaemia (Hb 8.5), abdominal distension and a mobile mass → right-sided (caecal) carcinoma (bleeds occultly, rarely obstructs).

why.A: An abdominal-wall tumour doesn't cause iron-deficiency anaemia.
why.C: Descending colon cancer obstructs early and gives a change in bowel habit.
why.D: Diverticular disease doesn't cause a mass with chronic anaemia.

stem: A 70 year old lady presents to the hospital with a history of passing bright red blood mixed with stool for 3 weeks. Review of systems reveals low appetite, constipation and approximately 4kg weight loss in 2 months. She denies abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and fever, but she feels lethargic. On examination, she is pale. Vital signs: BP: 110/70, pulse 92/min and temperature: 37, and oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Elderly patient, rectal bleeding mixed with stool, change in bowel habit, weight loss and anemia → colorectal cancer until proven otherwise.

why.C: Diverticulitis presents with LLQ pain and fever.
why.D: IBD usually presents younger with diarrhea.

stem: Rectal cancer stage T3c N1 with no mets, given chemoradiation as neoadjuvant. the radiation role is:
expl: Neoadjuvant chemoradiation in T3 rectal cancer down-stages the tumor (making resection easier/sphincter-saving) and reduces local recurrence. Source key: down-stage.

why.B: Also a true benefit; the keyed answer is down-staging.
why.C: Radiation is local; it doesn't reduce distant recurrence.
why.D: Overall survival benefit is not proven.

stem: Neoadjuvant Radiotherapy role in colon cancer is?
expl: Radiotherapy is a local treatment → its role is local control (reducing local recurrence).

why.C: Systemic control is the role of chemotherapy.

stem: Woman with colon cancer underwent resection and had chemo after surgery. What is the type of chemo?
expl: Chemotherapy given after surgery = adjuvant.

why.C: Not a chemo type here.

stem: A 28 year old male presented to outpatient with 2 month history of bloody diarrhea. He was found to have hundreds of polyps in the colon and rectum on colonoscopy. What is the Best management?
srcNote: (Colorectal cancer?) might be more correct both B and C are viable options and can be chosen depending on the patient and the extensiveness of the polyps. Some articles say that if the number of polyps are <500 or <1000 then it’s preferred to do colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis. The source key includes uncertainty and discusses an alternative option; that original note is retained above.
expl: Hundreds of colorectal polyps in a young man = FAP → prophylactic restorative proctocolectomy with ileoanal pouch (removes all at-risk mucosa). Colectomy + IRA is an option if the rectum is relatively spared (needs lifelong surveillance).

why.A: Leaves the rectum with a permanent stoma.
why.B: An option if rectal polyps are few; not the best answer here.
why.C: Correct.
why.D: Removes everything but leaves a permanent ileostomy unnecessarily.

stem: A 65-year old man presented with abdominal pain, vomiting and constipation for 2 days. He was diagnosed with large bowel obstruction. He never had any abdominal surgery before. What is the most like etiology?
srcNote: Davidson 7th edition page 264: Large bowel obstruction from the most common: 1- colorectal adenocarcinoma 2- stricture diverticular disease 3- Sigmoid volvulus.
expl: Large-bowel obstruction in an older patient without previous surgery → colorectal adenocarcinoma (commonest), then diverticular stricture, then volvulus.

why.C: Second/third.
why.D: Hernias usually obstruct the small bowel.

stem: Which of the following is pre-malignant colorectal polyp?
expl: Adenomatous polyps (tubular, tubulovillous, villous) are premalignant — the adenoma–carcinoma sequence.

why.C: Hamartomas carry a low risk (except in syndromes).

stem: Which one of the following is a proven risk factor for colon cancer?
expl: Long-standing UC is a proven risk factor (risk rises after 8–10 years, especially pancolitis). Red meat is associated, but UC is the clearly proven one in the key.

why.C: Red meat is associated, but the key chose UC.

stem: A 67-year-old male presented with per-rectal bleeding since 6 months with unremarkable physical examination. Colonoscopy revealed ulcerating mass in the splenic flexure, confirmed by histopathology to be adenocarcinoma. Which of the following is recommended for staging of this cancer?

opts.t: CT scan chest, abdomen and pelvis

srcNote: (liver and splenic diseases and pancreatic masses)
expl: Colon cancer staging = CT chest, abdomen and pelvis (+ CEA). MRI pelvis is for rectal cancer.

why.C: Rectal cancer local staging.

stem: A 65 YO old otherwise fit man, presented with 2 days history of absolute constipation, abdominal pain and distension. CT scan shows a tumor involving sigmoid colon. What is the most appropriate management plan?
expl: Acute obstruction from a sigmoid tumour in a fit patient → Hartmann's procedure (resect, end colostomy, close the rectal stump) — removes the cancer and avoids an anastomosis in an unprepared, obstructed bowel.

why.A: A diverting colostomy leaves the tumour (for unfit/unresectable patients).
why.C: LAR is for rectal tumours.
why.D: APR is for low rectal tumours.
